flashcards.q: How does a CPU limit actually get enforced, and what's the default CFS period?
flashcards.a: Via the cgroup's CFS quota/period. Default period is 100ms; quota = limit x period (0.5 CPU limit = 50ms quota per 100ms period). Exceed the quota within one period and the container is throttled (paused) for the rest of that period.

flashcards.q: Why can a container show a healthy 60s average CPU graph while being badly throttled?
flashcards.a: CFS throttling happens per 100ms period, not per minute. Dozens of brief per-period throttle events can occur within a minute that looks fine on a smoothed average. Check container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total / container_cpu_cfs_periods_total instead.

flashcards.q: How does memory limit enforcement differ mechanically from CPU limit enforcement?
flashcards.a: Memory limits are a hard ceiling enforced by the kernel's cgroup OOM killer — exceed it and the container is killed immediately (exit 137), no throttling or grace period. CPU limits throttle (pause) instead of killing.

flashcards.q: What are the three Kubernetes QoS classes and their node-pressure eviction order?
flashcards.a: Guaranteed (requests==limits, both CPU+mem) evicted last; Burstable (requests set, differ from limits) evicted next; BestEffort (neither set) evicted first.

flashcards.q: Why is running HPA and VPA against the same metric an anti-pattern?
flashcards.a: VPA changing a pod's CPU request changes the denominator HPA computes utilization against, which can trigger HPA replica changes, which changes VPA's own usage observations — an oscillating feedback loop. Split responsibility instead (VPA on memory or Off mode, HPA on an independent metric).

flashcards.q: What can KEDA do that plain HPA structurally cannot, and why?
flashcards.a: Scale to zero replicas (minReplicaCount: 0). HPA's ratio-based algorithm needs at least one running replica to compute a metric against; KEDA adds a separate polling mechanism watching the external event source directly while the Deployment sits at zero.

flashcards.q: HPA defaults: sync interval and scaleDown stabilization window?
flashcards.a: Sync interval 15s by default. scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds commonly defaults to 300s to prevent flapping; scaleUp is near-immediate by default.

flashcards.q: What's the single most common reason Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter never scale up despite Pending pods?
flashcards.a: The pods have no resources.requests set. Both tools ignore zero-request pods entirely because they can't determine resource shortage is the actual blocker.

flashcards.q: Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter — provisioning time and mechanism?
flashcards.a: Cluster Autoscaler scales pre-defined node groups (ASG/MIG), ~4-8 min to Ready. Karpenter calls cloud provisioning APIs directly for the best-fit instance type, ~45-60s, plus continuous consolidation for bin-packing.

flashcards.q: How are GPUs requested in Kubernetes by default, and are they fractionally shareable?
flashcards.a: Via the device plugin framework as an extended resource (nvidia.com/gpu) expressed only as a limit, in whole non-fractional units. No built-in fractional allocation — sharing requires MIG (hardware partition, isolated) or time-slicing (software, no isolation).

flashcards.q: A GPU pod is Pending despite a GPU node showing free capacity. Most likely cause?
flashcards.a: Missing toleration for the GPU node pool's taint (e.g. nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule) — GPU nodes are near-universally tainted to keep ordinary workloads off them.

flashcards.q: Why does a service mesh sidecar complicate HPA/VPA sizing?
flashcards.a: HPA computes CPU utilization against total pod CPU (app + sidecar), so sidecar overhead shifts scale-out triggers; VPA recommendations for the app container alone can undercount real pod-level needs if sidecar footprint isn't accounted for separately.
